What is Git: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in source code, enabling collaboration and history management. GitHub is a cloud platform for hosting Git repositories.

git --version
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git init & clone: Create a new local repository with git init, or copy an existing remote repository using git clone with HTTPS or SSH URLs.

git init my-project
cd my-project
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
git clone git@github.com:user/repo.git
git add & commit: Stage changes with git add and record them in history with git commit. The staging area lets you craft precise commits with meaningful messages.

git add file.txt
git add .
git commit -m "Add initial setup"
git commit -am "Update readme"
git status & log: git status shows the current state of working directory and staging area. git log displays commit history with various formatting options.

git status
git log
git log --oneline --graph --all
git log --oneline -5
git diff: Compare changes between working directory, staging area, and commits. Use diff to review changes before staging or committing.

git diff
git diff --staged
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD
git diff branch1..branch2
Config levels: Git config has three levels: system (all users), global (your account), local (per-repo). Each level overrides the one above. Use --list to view all settings.

git config --system --list
git config --global --list
git config --local --list
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
Git Aliases: Create shortcuts for frequent commands using git config alias. Aliases can chain commands and accept arguments for powerful shorthand.

git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.br branch
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all"
git config --global alias.unstage "reset HEAD --"
git lg  # uses alias
gitignore deep: The .gitignore file uses glob patterns to exclude files. Negate patterns with !, ignore directories with trailing /, and use ** for nested patterns. Global gitignore applies to all repos.

# .gitignore examples
node_modules/
*.log
!important.log  # override negation
build/**/*.o
# Global gitignore:
git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global
gitattributes: The .gitattributes file controls how Git handles files per-path: line endings (CRLF vs LF), diff drivers, merge strategies, and language detection. Essential for cross-platform teams.

# .gitattributes
*.js text eol=lf
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.png binary
*.pbxproj merge=union
*.txt linguist-language=Text
Hook basics: Git hooks are scripts in .git/hooks/ that trigger on actions like commit, push, or merge. Client hooks (pre-commit, prepare-commit-msg) and server hooks (pre-receive, post-receive) enforce policies.

# .git/hooks/pre-commit (make executable)
#!/bin/sh
npm run lint || exit 1

# Skip hooks temporarily:
git commit --no-verify
git push --no-verify
git worktree: Worktrees let you check out multiple branches simultaneously in separate directories. Share the same repository but maintain independent working directories and index files.

git worktree add ../hotfix hotfix-branch
git worktree add -b feature/new ../feature-new main
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../hotfix

git branch:
Branches are lightweight pointers to commits. List, create, rename, and delete branches to isolate work on features or fixes.

Visual:
main  ●──●──●──●
            \
feature      ●──●──●
Each branch is just a pointer. Creating a branch doesn't copy files — it just creates a new label.

git branch
git branch feature-login
git branch -d old-branch
git branch -m old-name new-name
git checkout & switch: Switch between branches using checkout or the newer switch command. checkout can also restore files from history.

git checkout main
git switch feature-login
git checkout -b new-branch
git switch -c new-branch
git merge:
Integrate changes from one branch into another. Fast-forward merges apply commits directly; three-way merges create a merge commit.

Merge vs Rebase:
MERGE (preserves history)
main  ●──●──●──●──●
         \    /
feature   ●──●

REBASE (linear history)
main  ●──●──●──●──●
               /
feature       ●──●
Merge keeps ancestor relationships; rebase rewrites history for a clean line.

git switch main
git merge feature-login
git merge --no-ff feature-login
Merge conflicts: When parallel changes conflict, Git marks the file. Manually edit to resolve, then stage and commit the resolution.

# Edit file to resolve <<<<<<< markers
git add resolved-file.txt
git merge --continue
git merge --abort
Merge strategies: Git supports multiple merge strategies: recursive (default for two branches), octopus (multiple branches), ours (keep current), subtree. Pass -s to select strategy and -X for options.

git merge -s recursive -X theirs feature
git merge -s ours feature
git merge -s octopus branch1 branch2 branch3
git merge -X patience feature
Squash merge: Squash merging combines all commits from a feature branch into a single new commit on the target branch. Cleaner history but loses granular commit details.

# On GitHub: select "Squash and merge"
# Locally:
git merge --squash feature-branch
git commit -m "feat: add complete feature"
merge --squash vs squash merge: merge --squash stages all changes without committing (you commit manually). GitHub's squash merge auto-commits. Both flatten history; use when granular commits lack individual value.

# merge --squash (manual commit required):
git checkout main
git merge --squash feature
git commit -m "Add everything"

# What it does: apply all diffs, none of the commits
git merge-tree: merge-tree computes the three-way merge result without touching the index or working tree. Useful for previewing merge outcomes or scripting merge logic.

git merge-tree main feature
git merge-tree --write-tree main feature
git merge-tree -z main feature | xargs -0
Orphan branches: Orphan branches share no commit history with the current branch. Useful for things like gh-pages, documentation, or starting a project in a subdirectory with separate history.

git checkout --orphan gh-pages
git rm -rf .
git commit --allow-empty -m "Initial orphan commit"
git push origin gh-pages

git rebase:
Reapply commits from one branch onto another tip for a linear history. Use interactive rebase to squash, reorder, or edit commits.

Visual:
BEFORE:
main    A──B──C
         \
feature  D──E

AFTER rebase:
main    A──B──C
               \
feature        D'──E'
D' and E' are NEW commits (different hashes). The original D/E still exist until garbage collected. Rebase rewrites history — never rebase shared/pushed branches.

git rebase main
git rebase -i HEAD~3
git rebase --continue
git rebase --abort
Interactive rebase (fixup, reword, drop,: Interactive rebase opens an editor where you choose actions per commit: pick (keep), reword (edit message), edit (amend content), squash (combine with previous), fixup (squash discarding message), drop (delete), exec (run command).

git rebase -i HEAD~5
# Commands:
# pick abc123 Add feature
# fixup def456 WIP
# reword 789ghi Fix typo
# exec npm test  # run between commits
# drop 012jkl Broken commit
# squash 345mno Combine with previous
Rebase strategies: Rebase offers strategies like --rebase-merges (preserve merge commits), --strategy recursive, --strategy-option theirs for conflict resolution, and --ignore-date to reset timestamps.

git rebase --rebase-merges main
git rebase -s recursive -X theirs main
git rebase --ignore-date main
git rebase --committer-date-is-author-date main
rebase --onto: rebase --onto replays commits onto a different base than upstream. Extract a feature branch from the wrong parent, or move a sub-branch to start from a different point.

# Move feature (based on wrong-branch) to main:
git rebase --onto main wrong-branch feature

# Cherry-pick a range onto a new base:
git rebase --onto main old-base feature
Autosquash: Autosquash automatically arranges fixup! and squash! commits during interactive rebase. Combined with git commit --fixup/--squash, it streamlines fixup workflows.

git commit --fixup abc123  # creates "fixup! original msg"
git commit --squash def456  # creates "squash! original msg"
git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~5

# One-liner fixup:
git commit --fixup abc123 && git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~3
When NOT to rebase: Never rebase commits that exist on a shared/public branch. Rebase rewrites history — anyone who pulled your old branch will have divergent history. The bane of rebasing is the force push that breaks collaborators.

# GOLDEN RULE:
# If others have pulled your branch, DO NOT rebase it.
# Instead: merge or revert.

# If you MUST rebase a pushed branch (solo dev):
git push --force-with-lease origin feature

# Safer alternative:
git merge main

git stash: Temporarily save uncommitted changes to clean your working directory. Apply, drop, or list stashes to manage WIP context switches.

git stash
git stash push -m "WIP login form"
git stash list
git stash pop
git stash drop stash@{0}
Stash deep: Stashes are stored as commits on the reflog of refs/stash. --include-untracked or --all captures untracked/ignored files. Stash show inspects contents without applying.
Partial stash: Stash only specific files or hunks with --patch for interactive selection. You can also stash individual pathspecs using git stash push -- <path> since Git 2.13.

git stash push -m "Only src changes" -- src/
git stash push --patch -m "Selective hunks"
git stash push -m "Modules only" -- "*.py"
git stash --  # deprecated form
Stash across branches: Stash is not branch-specific — you can stash on one branch and pop on another. Git auto-merges if changes apply cleanly; conflicts are handled manually.

git switch feature
git stash push -m "WIP on feature"
git switch main
git stash pop  # applies feature's WIP to main

# Check stash origin branch:
git stash list --format="%gd %gs (%an)"
Create branch from stash: Turn a stash into a proper branch with git stash branch. This creates a new branch starting at the commit where the stash was originally created.

git stash branch new-feature-branch stash@{0}

# Without specifying stash, uses the latest:
git stash branch new-feature-branch

# Equivalent to:
# git checkout -b new-feature-branch <stash-origin-commit>
# git stash pop

git reset & revert: Reset moves branch pointers (soft, mixed, hard). Revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous commit, safe for shared history.

git reset HEAD~1
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git revert HEAD
git revert abc123
Reset modes deep (--soft, --mixed, --har: --soft: moves HEAD only (changes stay staged). --mixed (default): moves HEAD and unstages changes (working tree unchanged). --hard: moves HEAD, unstages, and discards working tree changes. --hard is DESTRUCTIVE.

# Starting with staged + unstaged changes:
git reset --soft HEAD~1  # commits undone, changes STAY staged
git reset --mixed HEAD~1 # commits undone, changes UNSTAGED
git reset --hard HEAD~1  # commits gone, changes DISCARDED

# Safety: use --hard only if you're sure
git restore: Restore is the modern alternative to checkout for restoring files. Restore working tree from index (default) or a specific commit. --staged un stages, --source <tree> picks from a commit.

git restore file.txt          # discard working tree changes
git restore --staged file.txt  # unstage
git restore --source HEAD~2 file.txt  # restore from old version
git restore -SW .  # unstage AND discard all changes
git switch: Switch is the modern alternative to checkout for branch operations. Cleaner semantics: switch branches, detach with --detach, create with -c, and return to previous with @{-1}.

git switch main
git switch -c new-feature
git switch --detach HEAD~3
git switch -  # previous branch
git switch -c bug-fix @{-1}
Reflog deep: The reflog is Git's safety net — it records every HEAD movement including resets, rebases, and merges. Entries expire in 90 days (30 for unreachable). Use it to recover from almost any mistake.

git reflog                         # view history
git reflog show main               # branch-specific reflog
git reflog --date=iso              # with timestamps
git reset --hard HEAD@{2}          # go back to earlier state
git checkout main@{one.week.ago}   # time travel

# Expiry config:
git config gc.reflogExpire 180.days
Orphan commits: Orphan commits have no parent (root commits). The first commit in a repo is always an orphan. Create new root commits for independent history lines like gh-pages or separate documentation.

# First commit = orphan by definition
git log --all --max-parents=0 HEAD  # find root commits

# Create an orphan branch:
git checkout --orphan docs
git rm -rf .
git commit --allow-empty -m "root"

# Preserve orphan with git replace:
git replace --graft <orphan-hash> <parent-hash>
filter-branch vs filter-repo: git filter-branch rewrites history en masse but is slow and dangerous. git filter-repo is the recommended replacement — faster, safer, and designed for large-scale history rewrites like purging secrets or splitting repos.

# OLD (filter-branch - deprecated):
git filter-branch --force --index-filter \
  'git rm --cached --ignore-unmatch secrets.txt' \
  --prune-empty -- --all

# NEW (filter-repo - recommended):
git filter-repo --path secrets.txt --invert-paths
git filter-repo --path src/ --path tests/
git filter-repo --strip-blobs-bigger-than 10M

# After filter-repo, push with:
git remote add origin <url>
git push --force --all

git remote: Remotes are references to remote repository URLs. Manage connections to push, pull, and fetch from collaboration sources.

git remote -v
git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git remote rename origin upstream
git remote remove origin
git push & pull:
Push local commits to a remote branch and pull (fetch + merge) remote changes into your current branch. Set upstream for convenience.

Push vs Pull vs Fetch:
LOCAL                     REMOTE
●──●──●  push ——————→  ●──●──●
●──●──●  ←————— pull   ●──●──●
●──●──●  ←—— fetch ——  ●──●──●
        (no merge)

PUSH  = upload + merge to remote
PULL  = fetch + merge (may conflict)
FETCH = download only (review first)
Always pull before push to avoid rejection. Use `git pull --rebase` for cleaner history.

git push origin main
git push -u origin feature
git pull
git pull --rebase
git fetch:
Download commits, files, and references from a remote without merging. Use fetch to review changes before integrating.

Fetch vs Pull:
FETCH: origin/main updated, main stays
main     ●──●──●──●
             \
origin/main  ●──●──●──●

PULL: origin/main updated AND merged
main     ●──●──●──●──●──●
                       (merge commit)
Fetch is safe — it never changes your working tree. Always fetch before push to check for remote changes.

git fetch origin
git fetch --all
git log origin/main
git diff main origin/main
Pull Requests: PRs propose changes from a fork or branch for review before merging. Include descriptions, reviewers, and link to issues for context.

# Create a branch, push, then open PR on GitHub
git switch -b fix-bug
git push -u origin fix-bug
# Then open PR at github.com/user/repo/pulls
Pull request workflow:
The full PR lifecycle: fork/clone → branch → commit → push → open PR → request reviewers → address feedback → update branch → merge. Draft PRs signal work-in-progress.

PR Lifecycle:
Fork → Clone → Branch → Commit → Push → PR (Draft) → 
  ↓
Request Review → Address Feedback → Update Branch →
  ↓
Approve → Merge (Squash/Rebase/Merge) → Delete Branch
Use draft PRs for early feedback. Update the branch with more commits or rebase — avoid force pushes on shared PR branches.

# Full PR workflow:
git switch -c feat/new-button
git commit -m "Add new button"
git push -u origin feat/new-button
# Open PR via:
gh pr create --title "feat: add new button" --body "Closes #42"

# Update PR:
git push origin feat/new-button  # adds commits automatically
Code review: Code review is the process of examining code changes before merging. Focus on correctness, style, design, and test coverage. Use inline comments, suggestion blocks, and review approval flows.

# CLI review flow:
gh pr checkout 42
git diff main...HEAD

# Suggested changes:
# ```suggestion
# const newValue = 42;
# ```

# Approve:
gh pr review --approve --body "LGTM!"
gh pr review --request-changes --body "Fix edge case"
Merge queue: Merge queues group PRs and test them together before merging to main. Prevents semver conflicts where individual PRs pass CI but fail when combined. Available on GitHub with merge queues beta.

# .github/merge-queue.yml
merge_strategy:
  method: squash
  required_checks:
    - 'Tests (ubuntu-latest)'
    - 'Lint'

# PR comment to add to queue:
/queue
PR & Issue templates: Templates standardize PR and issue creation with YAML frontmatter or Markdown forms. Use checkboxes, dropdowns, and text areas to gather consistent information.

# .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md
---
name: Bug fix
about: Fix a bug
---

## Description
<!-- What does this PR fix? -->

## Testing
- [ ] Unit tests pass
- [ ] Manual QA

## Closes
Fixes #42

# .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug.yml
name: Bug Report
description: File a bug report
body:
  - type: textarea
    attributes:
      label: Steps to reproduce
GH CLI deep: The gh CLI provides full GitHub workflow from the terminal: create PRs, manage issues, run workflows, review code, and manage releases. Use gh extension for custom functionality.

gh auth login
github repo create my-app --public --clone
github pr create --title "Feature" --body "Closes #12" --assignee @me
github pr review 42 --approve
github run list --workflow=test.yml
github release create v1.0.0 --notes "First release"
github issue list --label bug
github extension install gh-metrics

git cherry-pick: Apply specific commits from one branch onto another. Useful for selective porting of changes without merging entire branches.

git cherry-pick abc123
git cherry-pick abc123..def456
git cherry-pick --continue
git cherry-pick --abort
Sparse checkout: Sparse checkout lets you work with only a subset of files in the working tree. Ideal for monorepos where you only need specific directories. Combined with cone mode for performance.

git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/user/monorepo.git
cd monorepo
git sparse-checkout init --cone
git sparse-checkout set apps/web packages/shared
git sparse-checkout add docs

# Without clone:
git sparse-checkout init --cone
git sparse-checkout set src/
Shallow & deep clone: Shallow clones (--depth 1) fetch only the latest commits — fast for CI. Deep clones fetch full history. --depth=N fetches N commits. --shallow-since filters by date.

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> fastest clone, no history

git clone --depth 5 https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> last 5 commits

git clone --shallow-since="2024-01-01" https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> commits since date

# Unshallow later:
git fetch --unshallow
Partial clone: Partial clones defer downloading blob data until needed. --filter=blob:none skips all blobs at clone time — files are fetched on checkout. --filter=tree:0 skips trees too. Dramatically reduces clone time.

git clone --filter=blob:none https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> fast clone, 90% less data
# -> files downloaded on git checkout/restore

git clone --filter=tree:0 https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> even lighter: trees fetched on dir access

git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> metadata only
git bundle: Bundle packs commits and refs into a single file for offline transport. Transfer via USB, email, or air-gapped networks. The receiver can pull or fetch from the bundle as if it were a remote.

# Create bundle:
git bundle create repo.bundle HEAD main
git bundle create update.bundle --since=2.weeks main

# Receive:
git clone repo.bundle dest-dir
git fetch update.bundle main

# Verify:
git bundle verify update.bundle
git bundle list-heads update.bundle
git archive: Export a snapshot of the repository as a tar or zip archive without the .git directory. Perfect for distribution, deployments, or sharing code without history.

git archive --format=zip HEAD > project.zip
git archive --format=tar HEAD | gzip > project.tar.gz
git archive --format=zip -o latest.zip main
git archive --prefix=project-v1.0/ HEAD | gzip > v1.0.tar.gz
git bisect run: Bisect run automates git bisect by passing a script that exits 0 (good) or non-zero (bad). Git will binary-search the range and find the first bad commit automatically.

# Manual:
git bisect start HEAD v1.0.0
git bisect run npm test

# Script approach:
git bisect start HEAD v1.0.0 --
git bisect run ./test-bug.sh

# test-bug.sh:
# #!/bin/bash
# npm run build && npm test

# Result: first commit where test fails
git blame & annotations: git blame annotates each line with the commit, author, and date that last modified it. Useful for tracking when/why a change was made. -L limits to line range; -w ignores whitespace.

git blame file.txt
git blame -L 10,30 file.txt
git blame -w -C -C file.txt  # detect moved lines
git log -p -S "search-term" -- file.txt  # search commit content

# Annotations via blame ignore revs:
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs
git grep: git grep searches files in any revision, not just working tree. Faster than system grep by limiting to tracked files. Supports regex, line numbers, file names, and context.

git grep "TODO"
git grep -n "function" -- *.js
git grep -c "class" HEAD~5  # count matches at old revision
git grep --cached "TODO"     # search staged
git grep -e "import" --and -e "from"  # multi-pattern

Blob objects: Blobs store file content identified by SHA-1 hash. The blob hash is deterministic — same content always produces the same hash (content-addressable). Blobs don't store filenames — that's the tree's job.

echo "hello" | git hash-object --stdin -w
git hash-object -w file.txt
git cat-file -p <blob-hash>
git cat-file -t <blob-hash>  # prints "blob"
Tree objects: Trees represent directory snapshots. A tree maps filenames → blob hashes (files) or sub-tree hashes (directories), plus permissions. Trees are also content-addressed by hash.

git cat-file -p main^{tree}
git cat-file -p HEAD:src/
git ls-tree HEAD
git ls-tree -r HEAD  # recursive

# Create a tree manually:
git write-tree  # creates tree from current index
Commit objects: A commit is a snapshot pointer containing: tree hash (root directory), parent commit hash(es), author/committer info, timestamp, and message. The commit hash is what you see in git log.

git cat-file -p HEAD
git cat-file -t HEAD  # prints "commit"

# Inspect commit structure:
# tree <root-tree-hash>
# parent <parent-commit-hash>
# author Name <email> timestamp
# committer Name <email> timestamp
#
# Commit message

git log --format=raw HEAD
Packfiles: Git stores objects in two forms: loose (individual files in .git/objects/) and packed (efficient deltas in .git/objects/pack/). Packfiles compress objects using delta encoding — storing only differences between versions.

git gc  # pack loose objects
git count-objects -v  # see loose vs packed
git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/*.idx | head -30
git repack -ad  # repack everything
git prune  # remove unreachable loose objects
git gc: Garbage collection packs loose objects into packfiles and prunes unreachable objects. Auto-runs on threshold (6700 loose objects). Manual gc optimizes repository size and performance.

git gc  # auto mode
git gc --aggressive  # slower, better compression
git gc --prune=now   # remove all unreachable
git gc --auto        # only if needed

# Config:
git config gc.auto 5000
git config gc.aggressiveWindow 250
git fsck: Filesystem check verifies repository integrity by scanning all objects and references. Detects dangling blobs, missing objects, and corruption. Run after hardware failures or suspicious behavior.

git fsck
git fsck --full     # check all objects
git fsck --lost-found  # recover dangling objects

git fsck --unreachable  # show unreachable

# Repair dangling objects:
git fsck --lost-found  # results in .git/lost-found/
git rev-parse: rev-parse resolves any Git revision specifier to a SHA-1 hash. Parse branch names, tags, relative refs (HEAD~3), dates (@{yesterday}), or ranges. Essential for scripting and plumbing.

git rev-parse HEAD
git rev-parse main
git rev-parse HEAD~3
git rev-parse @{yesterday}
git rev-parse HEAD:src/index.js

git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD  # branch name
git rev-parse --show-toplevel    # repo root
git cat-file: cat-file is the primary plumbing command to inspect Git objects. Pass type flag (-t), size (-s), pretty-print (-p), or check existence (-e). View any object by hash or revision.

git cat-file -p HEAD       # pretty-print commit
git cat-file -p abc123     # print any object
git cat-file -t abc123     # blob | tree | commit
git cat-file -s abc123     # object size in bytes

git cat-file --batch-check < hashes.txt  # batch mode
git cat-file --batch-all-objects --unordered | head

Actions (CI/CD): GitHub Actions automates workflows (test, build, deploy) triggered by events like push, PR, or schedule. Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows/.

# .github/workflows/test.yml
name: Tests
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm install && npm test
Workflow syntax: Workflow YAML defines triggers (on), jobs (parallel by default), steps (sequential), actions (reusable units), and expressions (${{ }}). Use if: conditionals, concurrency groups, and environment targets.

name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    paths: ['src/**']
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      env:
        type: choice
        options: [staging, production]

jobs:
  build:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    concurrency: ci-${{ github.ref }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Event: ${{ github.event_name }}"
Matrix builds: Matrix strategies run the same job across multiple configurations (OS, version, environment). Use include to add variants, exclude to remove, and fail-fast to cancel all on failure.

jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        node: [18, 20, 22]
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            node: 20
            coverage: true
        exclude:
          - os: windows-latest
            node: 22
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      - run: npm test
      - if: matrix.coverage
        run: npm run coverage
Reusable workflows: Call a workflow from another workflow using the uses keyword with secrets and inputs. Reusable workflows reduce duplication across repos. They must be in a public repo or same org.

# Caller workflow:
jobs:
  call-lint:
    uses: org/shared-workflows/.github/workflows/lint.yml@v1
    with:
      node-version: 20
    secrets:
      token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

# Reusable workflow (lint.yml):
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      node-version:
        type: string
        required: true
    secrets:
      token:
        required: true
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run lint
Environment protection: GitHub Environments add protection rules: required reviewers, wait timers, and deployment branch restrictions. Combined with secrets per-environment for secure deployments.

# Create environment via UI: Settings > Environments

# Workflow using environments:
jobs:
  deploy:
    environment:
      name: production
      url: https://app.example.com
    steps:
      - run: deploy.sh
        env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PRODUCTION_API_KEY }}

# Protected: requires approval before deploy
Self-hosted runners: Self-hosted runners run Actions on your own infrastructure. Register at repo/org/enterprise level. Use labels for routing. Ideal for custom hardware, internal networks, or cost savings at scale.

# Register a runner:
# Settings > Actions > Runners > Add runner
./config.sh --url https://github.com/user/repo --token ABC123
./run.sh

# Workflow targeting self-hosted:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64, gpu]
    steps:
      - run: nvidia-smi

# Scale sets: use actions/actions-runner-controller on Kubernetes
OIDC: OpenID Connect (OIDC) lets workflows authenticate to cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP, HashiCorp) without storing long-lived secrets. Exchange a JWT token for temporary cloud credentials.

# AWS example:
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456:role/GitHubActions
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: aws s3 sync ./dist s3://my-bucket

# Azure:
# - uses: Azure/login@v1
#   with:
#     client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
#     tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
#     allow-no-subscriptions: true

Issues & Projects: GitHub Issues track bugs, features, and tasks. Projects organize issues into boards with columns for planning and tracking work.

# Create via GitHub UI
github issue create --title "Bug" --body "Description"
github issue list
github issue view 42
GitHub Pages: Host static websites directly from a repository. Configure source branch and folder in Settings, then access at username.github.io/repo.

# Enable in Settings > Pages
# Build and deploy action:
# - uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3
#   with:
#     github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
#     publish_dir: ./dist
Forks & Upstream:
Fork a repository to contribute without direct write access. Sync your fork by adding the original repo as an upstream remote.

Fork + Upstream Flow:
UPSTREAM (original/repo)
  ●──●──●
    ↑ fork (copy on GitHub)
ORIGIN (your/repo on GitHub)
  ●──●──●
    ↑ clone
LOCAL (your machine)
  ●──●──●
    ↑ add upstream remote
  ●──●──●──●  (sync from upstream)
Use `origin` for your fork, `upstream` for the original. Send PRs from your fork back to upstream.

# Fork via GitHub UI, then:
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original/repo.git
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge upstream/main
git push
Projects (Beta): GitHub Projects provides spreadsheet-style project tracking with custom fields, views (table, board, roadmap), and automation. Link issues/PRs across repos in a single org-level project.

# Create via UI: Projects > New project
# Or via GraphQL API:
gh project create owner --title "Sprint Q2" --template "Team planning"
gh project item-add owner 42 --repo owner/repo --issue 123

# Fields: Iteration, Single Select, Text, Number, Date, Tracks
# Automation: Status = "In Progress" when PR opened
Discussions: GitHub Discussions provide a forum-style space for Q&A, ideas, and announcements — separate from the issue tracker. Useful for community engagement, RFCs, and collective decision-making.

# Create via GitHub UI: Discussions tab

# Categorize:
# - Q&A (mark accepted answer)
# - Ideas (convert to issue)
# - Announcements (locked)
# - General

# Link discussion in PR:
gh pr create --title "RFC: new API" --discussion 42
Codespaces: GitHub Codespaces provides cloud-hosted development environments configured by a devcontainer.json file. Start, stop, and customize VSCode environments from any browser or VS Code.
Dependabot: Dependabot automates dependency updates by scanning manifest files and opening PRs for out-of-date packages. Configure version strategies, schedule, and reviewers in dependabot.yml.

# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "npm"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
      day: "monday"
    versioning-strategy: increase
    open-pull-requests-limit: 10
    reviewers:
      - "team-maintainers"
    labels:
      - "dependencies"
  - package-ecosystem: "docker"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "monthly"
Secret scanning & code scanning: Secret scanning detects exposed credentials (keys, tokens) in repos. Code scanning (CodeQL) finds vulnerabilities via static analysis. Both integrate into PR checks to prevent merging insecure code.

# Enable: Settings > Security > Code security

# CodeQL workflow:
# .github/workflows/codeql.yml
name: CodeQL
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  analyze:
    uses: github/codeql-action/.github/workflows/codeql-analysis.yml@v3

# Secret scanning is automatic on public repos.
# Custom patterns for private repos:
# Settings > Security > Secret scanning > Custom patterns
Branch protection rules: Branch protection rules enforce workflows: require PRs, status checks, up-to-date branches, signed commits, or specific reviewers. Essential for main branch security and compliance.

# Configure: Settings > Branches > Add rule
# Branch name pattern: main, release/*
# Protect matching branches:
#  ☑ Require a pull request before merging
#    ☑ Require approvals (1-6)
#  ☑ Require status checks
#    ☑ Require branches up-to-date
#  ☑ Require conversation resolution
#  ☑ Require signed commits
#  ☑ Require linear history
#  ☑ Allow force pushes (with restrictions)
#  ☑ Allow deletions

# Via API:
gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/main/protection \
  --method PUT --input protection.json

GitLab CI: GitLab CI uses .gitlab-ci.yml with stages, jobs, and runners. Supports Kubernetes integration, auto DevOps, and built-in container registry. Jobs run in isolated environments.

# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages:
  - test
  - build
  - deploy

test:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm install
    - npm test
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml

build:
  stage: build
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"
  script:
    - npm run build

deploy:
  stage: deploy
  environment: production
  script:
    - kubectl apply -f deploy/
BitBucket Pipelines: BitBucket Pipelines uses bitbucket-pipelines.yml for CI/CD with built-in Docker support and deployment environments. Integrates with Jira for traceable deployments.

# bitbucket-pipelines.yml
image: node:20

pipelines:
  default:
    - step:
        name: Test
        caches:
          - node
        script:
          - npm install
          - npm test
  branches:
    main:
      - step:
          name: Deploy
          deployment: production
          script:
            - npm run build
            - pipe: atlassian/aws-s3-deploy:1.1.0
              variables:
                AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: $AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
                AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: $AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
Gerrit: Gerrit is a code review system for Git that uses a push-to-review workflow. Changes are pushed to refs/for/<branch> and must be reviewed and +2'ed before submission. Common in large-scale enterprise projects.

# Clone:
git clone ssh://user@gerrit:29418/project && scp -p gerrit:hooks/commit-msg .git/hooks/

# Push for review:
git push origin HEAD:refs/for/main

# Patch sets (amend existing change):
git commit --amend
git push origin HEAD:refs/for/main

# Review scores:
# -1/0/+1: Looks good (any reviewer)
# -2/+2: Approve (maintainer only)
# Submit: merge after approval
Git LFS: Git LFS (Large File Storage) replaces large files (binaries, assets, models) with text pointers in the repo while storing content on a remote server. Essential for game dev, ML, and design assets.

git lfs track "*.psd"
git lfs track "*.zip"
git add .gitattributes  # stores LFS patterns
git lfs migrate import --include="*.psd" --everything

# Clone with LFS:
git lfs clone https://github.com/user/repo.git

# Check LFS:
git lfs ls-files
git lfs status
Git submodules: Embed one repository inside another as a submodule. Pins a specific commit so the parent repo tracks exact dependency versions.

git submodule add https://github.com/user/lib.git lib
git submodule update --init --recursive
git submodule foreach git pull
git submodule status
Submodules vs subtrees: Submodules reference external repos as pointers; subtrees merge external code directly into your repo. Subtrees give you full control (no external dependency), submodules keep history separate. Choose subtrees for stability, submodules for active external development.

# Subtree add:
git subtree add --prefix lib/vendor https://github.com/user/lib.git main --squash

# Subtree pull:
git subtree pull --prefix lib/vendor https://github.com/user/lib.git main --squash

# Subtree push:
git subtree push --prefix lib/vendor origin vendor-branch

# Key difference:
# - Submodule: .gitmodules, commit pointer, needs --recursive clone
# - Subtree: files in your repo, no special clone needed
Monorepo strategies: Monorepos store multiple projects in a single repository. Strategies: Nx/Turborepo for JS, Bazel for polyglot, Gradle for JVM, and Pants for Python. Tooling handles selective builds and tests.

# Directory structure:
# apps/
#   web/
#   mobile/
#   admin/
# packages/
#   shared-ui/
#   utils/
#   types/
# tools/
#   ci/
#   scripts/

# Nx affected builds:
nx affected:test --base=main

# GitHub Actions path filtering:
on:
  push:
    paths:
      - 'apps/web/**'
      - 'packages/shared-ui/**'

Gitignore: The .gitignore file specifies intentionally untracked files (build artifacts, dependencies, env files) that Git should ignore.
Commit Messages: Write clear, conventional commit messages. Use imperative mood, capitalize first word, and include scope/tag for automatic changelogs.

# Conventional Commits
feat: add user login page
fix: resolve null pointer on profile load
chore: update dependencies
docs: improve API documentation
Branch Strategies: Common branching models: Git Flow (develop/release/hotfix), GitHub Flow (feature branches -> main), and trunk-based development for CI/CD.

# GitHub Flow:
# main (production-ready)
# feature/* (short-lived feature branches)
# Fix/merge via PR

# Git Flow:
# main, develop, feature/*, release/*, hotfix/*
Signing Commits: Sign commits with GPG or SSH keys to verify authorship. GitHub marks signed commits as Verified for trust and authenticity.

git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global user.signingkey KEY_ID
git commit -S -m "Signed commit"
git log --show-signature
Squashing Commits: Combine multiple commits into one for cleaner history. Use squash during merge on GitHub or interactive rebase locally.

git rebase -i HEAD~3
# Change 'pick' to 'squash' for commits to merge
git merge --squash feature-branch
git commit -m "Add complete feature"
Conventional commits: Conventional Commits specification standardizes commit messages: type(scope): description. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, ci, build, revert. Enables automatic versioning and changelog generation.

# Types:
# feat:     new feature (minor release)
# fix:      bug fix (patch release)
# BREAKING CHANGE: major release!
# chore:    maintenance
# docs:     documentation only
# refactor: code change without fix/feat
# perf:     performance improvement
# test:     adding/fixing tests
# ci:       CI/CD changes

feat(api): add user authentication endpoint
fix(ui): resolve button alignment on mobile

BREAKING CHANGE: removed deprecated v1 endpoints

# Tools: commitlint, standard-version, semantic-release
Semantic versioning with tags: Semantic versioning (semver): MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR = breaking changes, MINOR = features, PATCH = fixes. Tag releases with annotated tags and push them to trigger deployment workflows.

# Version bump examples:
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"
git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "Add user profiles (feature)"
git tag -a v1.1.1 -m "Fix login redirect (patch)"
git tag -a v2.0.0 -m "Rewrite API (breaking)"

# Push tags:
git push origin --tags

# Auto-tag with CI:
# GITHUB_REF will be refs/tags/v1.0.0
# Use semantic-release or similar for automation
Trivial merges: Trivial merges (fast-forward only) keep linear history without merge commits. Use when feature branches have a single commit or no divergent history. Configure branch settings to require linear history.

# Fast-forward only:
git merge --ff-only feature-branch
# -> Fails if branch has diverged

# PR settings (GitHub):
# Require linear history = "Rebase and merge" only

# Config:
git config --global merge.ff only

# Team convention:
# - Single-commit branch: rebase + fast-forward
# - Multi-commit branch: squash merge
Clean history: A clean Git history is readable, searchable, and bisectable. Guidelines: one logical change per commit, write descriptive messages, squash WIP/fixup commits, rebase before merging, avoid merge commits in feature branches.

# Before pushing, clean up:
git rebase -i HEAD~5
# - squash fixup! and WIP entries
# - reword unclear messages
# - drop broken commits

# Check bisect safety:
git bisect start HEAD v1.0
# Each commit should compile and pass tests

# .git-blame-ignore-revs for formatting commits:
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs
# Add formatting commit hashes there
Code review checklist: A systematic code review checklist covers: correctness (edge cases, error handling), security (input validation, auth), performance (N+1 queries, memory), style (project conventions), testing (coverage, meaningful tests), and documentation (API, README).

# Review checklist:
# [ ] Does the code work? (correctness)
# [ ] Are edge cases handled? (null, empty, errors)
# [ ] Is it secure? (injection, auth, secrets)
# [ ] Is it performant? (complexity, DB queries)
# [ ] Follows project conventions? (lint, style)
# [ ] Tests included and meaningful?
# [ ] Documentation updated? (README, API docs)
# [ ] No debugging code? (console.log, TODO)

# PR template checklist:
- [ ] I have added tests
- [ ] I have updated documentation
- [ ] My code follows project style
CI gates: CI gates are automated checks that block merging if they fail. Common gates: lint, type check, unit tests, integration tests, build, security scan, coverage threshold. Combine with branch protection to enforce.

# .github/workflows/ci-gates.yml
name: CI Gates
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run lint
  typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run typecheck
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run test -- --coverage
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run build
